summary: Describes the View-based Access Control Model for the SNMP architecture, which controls who can access which management information. It includes a MIB for managing its configuration. It obsoletes RFC 2275 and was replaced by RFC 3415.

eli5.summary: This decides which people may look at, or change, which parts of a device's information, like giving different keys to different workers.

questions: what is a mib view in snmp
how does snmp access control work
subtitle: How an SNMP agent decides who may read, write or be notified about which management data.

tldr.problem: An SNMP entity needs a way to check whether a given principal may read, write or send a particular piece of management information, and to restrict some users to only part of it.
tldr.mechanism: VACM maps a securityModel and securityName to a group, then uses the group, context, securityModel and securityLevel to find read, write and notify MIB views, and checks whether the requested object is in the selected view.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2575 obsoleted RFC 2275 and was itself replaced by RFC 3415.

today: RFC 2575 (a Draft Standard) is obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 3415. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2275.

sections.title: Where VACM Fits in SNMP
sections.content:
The SNMP architecture ([RFC2571]) describes an SNMP engine as a Dispatcher, a Message Processing Subsystem, a Security Subsystem and an Access Control Subsystem. The access control subsystem checks whether a specific type of access (read, write or notify) to a particular object instance is allowed.

This document defines one model for that subsystem, the View-based Access Control Model (VACM). The RFC notes that it is not necessarily the only access control model.

Access control happens when a Command Responder handles requests carrying Read Class and Write Class PDUs, and when a Notification Originator generates notifications. VACM provides services an application can call to check access rights, and it is the application's responsibility to make the proper calls. The access rights live in the engine's Local Configuration Datastore, and a MIB module in the document lets that data be configured remotely.
sections.eli5: A device keeps a rulebook about who may see or change what. This document describes one way to write and check that rulebook.

sections.title: Groups, Security Levels and Contexts
sections.content:
A group is a set of zero or more <securityModel, securityName> tuples on whose behalf management objects can be accessed. A group defines the access rights of every securityName in it, and a securityModel plus securityName maps to at most one group. VACM assumes the securityName has already been authenticated and does no authentication of its own.

The securityLevel (noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv or authPriv) lets a group have different rights at different levels of security. It must be passed in when access is checked.

An SNMP context is a collection of management information accessible by an SNMP entity. An item may exist in more than one context. VACM defines a vacmContextTable that lists the locally available contexts by contextName.
sections.eli5: People are put into teams, each team gets different rights depending on how carefully the person proved who they are, and the information is split into separate rooms called contexts.

sections.title: MIB Views and View Families
sections.content:
To limit what a group can see, access to a context goes through a MIB view: a specific set of managed object types, and optionally specific instances, within that context. A context will typically have one view covering everything and often others covering subsets.

Because objects are named by tree-like OBJECT IDENTIFIERs, a view is the union of view subtrees, where a subtree is all object instances sharing a common OBJECT IDENTIFIER prefix. To avoid needing very many subtrees, for example to cover one column of every row of a table, a family of view subtrees pairs an OBJECT IDENTIFIER (the family name) with a bit string (the family mask). The mask says which sub-identifiers of the name are significant. A family can be included in or excluded from a view.

For each context, group, securityModel and securityLevel, the access rights are given by three views: a read-view used for Read Class PDUs, a write-view used for Write Class PDUs, and a notify-view used when sending Notification Class PDUs.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving someone the whole filing cabinet, you can give them only certain drawers. The mask is a stencil that picks out the same slot in many similar folders at once.

sections.title: The isAccessAllowed Procedure
sections.content:
Applications call an abstract service, isAccessAllowed, with the securityModel, securityName, securityLevel, viewType (read, write or notify), contextName and variableName (the OID of the managed object). It returns a statusInformation value.

The checks run in order. The vacmContextTable must know the context, otherwise noSuchContext is returned. The vacmSecurityToGroupTable maps securityModel and securityName to a groupName, otherwise noGroupName. The vacmAccessTable, indexed by contextName, groupName, securityModel and securityLevel, must have an entry, otherwise noAccessEntry.

The entry holds the three views, and the viewType selects one. An empty view name or no configured view gives noSuchView. If the variableName is not in the selected MIB view the result is notInView, and otherwise accessAllowed.
sections.eli5: The device asks a series of questions: which room, which team, how well did you prove who you are, and is this item in your allowed list? Any missing answer means no entry.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
VACM assumes the calling module has already ensured the authentication and privacy that the passed securityLevel implies. When creating or deleting entries in the vacmViewTreeFamilyTable, it is important to follow the sequence recommended in that table's DESCRIPTION clause, otherwise unwanted access may be granted while the entries change.

The grouping of tuples in the vacmSecurityToGroupTable does not take securityLevel into account, so administrators should use the securityLevel index in the vacmAccessTable to separate noAuthNoPriv from authPriv and authNoPriv access.

A conformant implementation MUST implement the SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB according to vacmMIBCompliance and SHOULD implement the initial configuration in Appendix A. The MIB's objects control access to all MIB data and may be sensitive, so read and write access to them should be closely controlled.
sections.eli5: Change the rulebook in the right order, or someone might briefly get a key they should not have. And keep the rulebook itself locked up, because it controls everything else.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2275
sections.content:
RFC 2575 obsoleted RFC 2275. The change log lists mostly clarifications: extra text on when a vacmSecurityToGroupTable entry can be made active, REVISION clauses in the MODULE-IDENTITY, clearer text for the vacmAccessTable, and a DEFVAL clause for vacmAccessContextMatch.

It also uses the PDU Class terminology instead of RFC 1905 PDU types, and adds section 7.4 on access control to the MIB itself.
sections.eli5: This version mostly cleaned up unclear wording and added a note about protecting the rulebook itself.
